newsitem.title: USA: NPPC reimburses Pork Board $51,300 for checkoff.
newsitem.headline: NPPC reimburses Pork Board $51,300 for checkoff.

text.p: The National Pork Producers Council (NPPC) said on Friday it reimbursed the National Pork Board a total of $51,300 spent in the last year to monitor pork industry issues and groups.

The move came two days after the National Pork Board said it would support an Agriculture Department audit of the Pork Checkoff program, a promotion fund administered by the Board that included a grant to NPPC. NPPC came under fire earlier this year when it was revealed that some of the funds were used to monitor pork industry activists including environmentalists and animal rights groups by a consultant.

"While we continue to believe the monitoring was well within the parameters of the provisions of the Pork Act and Order, it is time that we put all the controversy surrounding this aside," NPPC president Jerry King said in a statement.

Under the federal Pork Act, 45 cents of every $100 of pork sold in the United States goes to the Pork Board as "checkoff" funds which are supposed to be used to support pork industry promotion, research and consumer information.
On March 28, the Agriculture Department ordered the Pork Board to recover any checkoff funds improperly spent.
King said the $51,300 represented "all money paid during the past year with checkoff funds for strategic issue monitoring."

"The monitoring was done by an outside consultant for NPPC and was limited to available public information on environmental, animal rights, industry structure and food safety issues," King said in the statement.
The reimbursement "in no way represents an admission of wrongdoing of any kind," King said.
NPPC officials have said the consultant, the firm of Mongoven Biscoe & Duchin Inc, was hired in 1996 and had written several reports on pork industry groups and issues.

The Mongoven firm was hired under an NPPC program, the Strategic Communications Initiative, aimed at pursuing what the NPPC called "accurate and fair reporting and coverage" of the pork industry, particularly by the news media.
Consumer groups have pressed in recent weeks for an accounting of how all checkoff funds were used.

"Checkoff funds, paid by family farmers, are being used to investigate the activities of organizations involving those same family farmers in efforts to enhance their farm future," Chuck Hassebrook of the Center for Rural Affairs said last week.
